name: No executive-approved AI policy
plainTerms: Nobody has written down what the company will and won't do with AI. Every team decides for itself, and no two teams decide the same way.

name: Policy not mapped to operations
plainTerms: There's a twelve-page AI policy. It lives in a shared drive. Nobody's day-to-day work changed when it was published.

name: No risk-tier taxonomy
plainTerms: Every AI project is treated the same. A tool that suggests lunch spots gets the same scrutiny as one that declines loan applications.
description: No agreed scheme exists for classifying AI use cases by risk, so every use case is implicitly treated as equivalent. Without tiers there is nothing to route on, nothing to scale review depth against, and no defensible basis for treating two use cases differently.
sectors: Cross-sector; foundational across all industries
indicators: No documented tier definitions or classification criteria | Review depth identical across materially different use cases | Reviewers unable to state which tier a given use case sits in | Risk language in policy that maps to no operational routing decision
rootCauses: Policy written before any volume of use cases existed to classify | Disagreement between functions about what counts as high risk, resolved by omitting the question | Concern that publishing tiers invites teams to argue their way into a lower one
mitigations: Define a small number of tiers with written classification criteria | Tie each tier to a concrete routing consequence, not just a label | Classify the existing portfolio retrospectively, not only new intake | Publish the criteria so classification can be challenged and is repeatable
reference: Precedes most other assessment failures. An organization without tiering cannot exhibit proportionate review, because there is nothing to be proportionate to.

name: Prohibited-use categories unenforced
plainTerms: The policy says the company will never use AI for a particular purpose. Nothing in any system actually prevents someone from doing it.

name: No accountable executive owner
plainTerms: Ask who owns AI risk and you get four names, a committee, and a shrug.

name: Policy unversioned / no change control
plainTerms: Someone edited the AI policy in March. Nobody can say what it said in February, or who changed it, or why.

name: Strategy–execution disconnect
plainTerms: Leadership announced an AI strategy. The projects actually being funded have very little to do with it.

name: No value measurement for the AI programme
plainTerms: The AI programme has been running eighteen months. When the CFO asks what it delivered, the answer is a list of projects, not a number — so at the next budget cycle, governance reads as pure cost.

name: Intake bypass
plainTerms: A team bought an AI tool on a corporate card, rolled it out to forty people, and the governance team found out when someone mentioned it in an unrelated meeting.
description: A use case reaches production without ever entering the governance intake process. It is never tiered, never reviewed, and never approved — so no downstream control in the lifecycle can attach to it.
sectors: Cross-sector
indicators: AI expenditure appearing with no corresponding intake record | SaaS AI features enabled without a change request | Model or API traffic originating from teams with no registered use case | Vendor renewal documentation describing capabilities absent from the register
rootCauses: Intake operates as a request rather than a gate, so nothing structurally prevents bypass | Procurement and governance workflows are not integrated | Intake is perceived as slow, so delivery teams route around it — see AGF-F027 and AGF-F037
mitigations: Integrate procurement with governance so AI expenditure triggers intake automatically | Scan for AI features newly enabled within the existing SaaS estate | Make the gate structural by tying it to funding release or access provisioning | Run amnesty-based discovery drives that surface existing bypasses without penalty | Address review throughput first — enforcement without a fast path drives bypass underground
reference: No single canonical public incident. Prevalence is supported by Verizon DBIR 2026 and IBM/Ponemon 2025 findings on unauthorized AI use.

name: Unsanctioned AI use
plainTerms: Half the department is pasting work into a free chatbot on their phones. It isn't on any list, because nobody ever decided to use it — people just started.
description: Individuals use unsanctioned AI tools on corporate data and devices, entirely outside any governance perimeter. Distinct from intake bypass in that no organizational adoption decision occurs at all — adoption is individual and invisible.
sectors: Cross-sector; consequences most acute in banking, biopharma, and insurance where the underlying data is regulated
indicators: Personal-account access to AI services from corporate devices | Cloud access security telemetry showing traffic to consumer AI domains | Expense claims for individual AI subscriptions | Sensitive document volume moving toward consumer AI endpoints
rootCauses: Sanctioned tooling is slower, less capable, or unavailable for the task | No approved-tool catalog exists, so there is nothing concrete to comply with | An enforcement-only posture drives usage further underground rather than eliminating it | Pent-up demand created by slow or opaque approval — see AGF-F037
mitigations: Provide fast sanctioned pathways rather than relying on prohibition alone | Apply redaction and data-loss controls at the egress point | Publish an approved-tool catalog with a genuinely fast addition process | Lead with amnesty-based discovery before enforcement
reference: Widely reported corporate source-code exposure through consumer AI assistants (2023) led to internal prohibitions at several large manufacturers. Netskope 2026 reports 47% of generative AI users on personal, unmanaged accounts.

name: Incomplete intake — context, data or owner missing
plainTerms: The intake form was submitted with 'TBD' for data sources and 'various' for the owner. It was approved anyway, because sending it back would have taken another three weeks.

name: No continuous or adaptive intake
plainTerms: Intake happens once a quarter in a big batch. Anything that comes up in between either waits three months or quietly skips the process.

name: Duplicate use cases undetected
plainTerms: Three teams built three versions of the same document summarizer. None of them knew about the others. All three went through review separately.

name: Vendor-supplied AI uncaptured in inventory
plainTerms: The HR system the company has used for years quietly added AI-driven candidate ranking in an update. It's now an AI system, but it's still filed as an HR system.
description: AI capability arrives inside software the organization already owns — a vendor adds a feature, enables a model, or ships an assistant in an update. The system remains registered under its original non-AI category, so no AI governance control ever attaches to it.
sectors: Cross-sector; heaviest exposure where core operational platforms are vendor-supplied
indicators: Vendor release notes describing AI capability with no corresponding governance event | Software categorized by original function rather than current capability | Contract renewals with AI terms for systems absent from the AI register | AI features enabled by default in existing tools with no configuration decision recorded
rootCauses: Inventory built once at procurement and never revisited as capability changed | No process watching vendor roadmaps or release notes for AI additions | Vendor management and AI governance operate as separate functions with no trigger between them | AI features enabled by default, so adoption requires no decision anyone records
mitigations: Add AI capability disclosure and change notification to vendor contract terms | Review vendor release notes against the register on a defined cadence | Re-screen the existing software estate for AI features rather than only assessing new purchases | Treat a vendor enabling AI capability as a governance event requiring re-intake | Require vendors to notify before enabling new AI capability, not after
reference: The dominant route by which regulated organizations acquire ungoverned AI. Distinct from unsanctioned use in that the organization bought the software deliberately; only the AI capability is unnoticed.

name: Agentic components not distinguished from models
plainTerms: The register says 'AI assistant.' It's actually an agent that can send emails and update records on its own — which is a completely different risk, recorded as if it were the same one.
description: Systems that can take actions — call tools, write to records, send communications, invoke other systems — are registered and governed as though they only produce text for a human to read. The risk profile of an agent differs fundamentally from that of a model, and the register cannot tell them apart.
sectors: Cross-sector; consequence rises sharply in banking and anywhere systems hold write access
indicators: Register entries describing capability in generic terms such as assistant or copilot | No field recording autonomy level, tool access, or write permissions | Systems with production write access whose governance record shows read-only assessment | No inventory of what actions a given deployment is permitted to take
rootCauses: Register schema designed before agentic deployment was common | Agentic capability added incrementally to a system already approved as a model | Vendor terminology obscures the distinction, and the register inherits it | No one has defined what autonomy levels the organization recognizes
mitigations: Record autonomy level, tool access, and write scope as mandatory register fields | Maintain an agent registry distinct from the model inventory | Require re-assessment when a system gains the ability to act rather than only to advise | Define recognized autonomy levels so the field has consistent meaning | Inventory permissions held by agent service accounts as part of assessment
reference: A classification gap created by rapid capability change rather than by process failure. The register is usually accurate as of the date it was designed.

name: Fragmented intake surfaces
plainTerms: Submitting an idea means filling out four different forms owned by four different teams, with most of the questions repeated across all of them. Most people fill out one and stop.

name: No triage or routing layer
plainTerms: An idea gets submitted, sits with the wrong team for two weeks, is forwarded to a second team, who forward it to a third. Nobody rejected it. It just circulated until the submitter gave up.
description: Submissions enter the organization with no upfront triage step that determines where they belong. Items route by guesswork, bounce between functions, and accumulate delay that is invisible in any single team's metrics because no single team ever held the item long enough to own the wait.
sectors: Cross-sector; worst where innovation, operational excellence, and AI governance run as separate intake channels
indicators: Submissions with multiple reassignments before first substantive review | Elapsed time far exceeding the sum of active review time | Submitters re-submitting the same idea through a different channel | No single queue where all incoming requests are visible
rootCauses: Multiple teams each built their own intake channel independently | No agreed criteria for which path a submission belongs on | Routing is a judgement call made by whoever receives the item first | Nobody owns the end-to-end submitter experience
mitigations: Establish a single upfront triage step preceding all routing decisions | Publish explicit routing criteria so classification is repeatable rather than discretionary | Make the full queue visible across functions so bouncing is observable | Measure and report elapsed time from submission, not active time per team | Assign ownership of the submission experience to a named role
reference: Manifests as submitter attrition and shadow adoption rather than as a reportable incident.

name: No consistent scoring methodology
plainTerms: Two reviewers assess similar projects and reach different conclusions, because the scoring criteria exist in their heads rather than on paper.

name: Tier assigned once, never revisited
plainTerms: A tool was rated low risk when it drafted internal emails. It now drafts customer communications. It is still rated low risk.

name: Miscategorization — high-impact rated low
plainTerms: A system that influences who gets hired was filed as a productivity tool, because it doesn't make the final call — a person does, after reading its ranking.

name: Transparency-triggering uses not flagged
plainTerms: Customers are chatting with an AI agent and nobody told them. Nothing in the assessment ever asked whether they would need to be told.
description: Use cases that trigger a legal duty to disclose AI involvement to an end user are not identified as such during assessment, so the disclosure obligation is never implemented anywhere downstream. Art. 50 applies by system function rather than risk tier, so the Annex III deferral provides no relief here.
sectors: Cross-sector; acute for organizations with EU-facing customers or operations
indicators: Customer-facing AI outputs carrying no disclosure language | No transparency-trigger field on the risk assessment form | AI-generated service or marketing content published without labelling | No record of which use cases touch EU data subjects
rootCauses: The assessment framework predates the transparency obligations and was never revised | Transparency treated as a legal question rather than an assessment field | Assumption that an internal-only classification excludes disclosure duties | Assumption that the high-risk deferral moved Art. 50 as well — it did not
mitigations: Add an explicit transparency-trigger question to the assessment form | Maintain a disclosure register mapped to individual use cases | Automate machine-readable marking where synthetic content is generated | Re-screen the existing portfolio rather than only new intake
reference: Art. 50 became enforceable 2 Aug 2026. Applies by system function, not risk tier, so mainstream generative deployments are in scope regardless of the Annex III deferral to Dec 2027.

name: No regulatory trigger built into assessment
plainTerms: The assessment asks thorough questions about data and security. It never asks which laws apply, so nobody finds out until someone in legal reads about it in the news.

name: Aggregate portfolio risk unassessed
plainTerms: Every individual AI project is low risk. Nobody has asked what it means that forty of them now depend on the same vendor's model.

name: Bias and fairness risk unassessed
plainTerms: A screening tool has been running for two years. Nobody has ever checked whether it treats different groups of applicants the same way.

name: Undifferentiated review burden
plainTerms: Every AI request — including one to summarize meeting notes — goes through the full security, architecture, privacy and legal review. It takes eleven weeks, the reviewers are drowning, and teams have quietly stopped asking.
description: Governance applies the same depth of review to every use case regardless of risk. The result is not more safety: reviewer capacity is consumed by low-risk items, genuinely high-risk items receive no additional attention because there is none left to give, and the delay drives teams out of the process entirely.
sectors: Cross-sector; most acute in regulated industries where review functions are already at capacity
indicators: Identical review path and duration across trivially and materially different use cases | Specialist review functions reporting sustained backlog | Review cycle times measured in months | Rising proportion of use cases discovered after deployment rather than at intake | Reviewers approving late-stage items without substantive examination in order to clear queue
rootCauses: Risk tiering was never established, or exists on paper without routing consequences — see AGF-F003 | Caution is expressed by adding reviewers rather than by directing them | No mechanism exists to route by risk, so the only safe default is to route everything everywhere | Fear that a fast path will be blamed if something goes wrong
mitigations: Establish tiered intake where low-risk use cases follow a materially shorter path | Route by questionnaire trigger so only the relevant specialist functions are engaged | Require attestation to core controls on the fast path, with sampled post-hoc validation | Measure reviewer load and cycle time per tier, and publish both | Treat sustained backlog as a governance failure in its own right rather than a resourcing complaint
reference: Presents as reviewer burnout and shadow adoption. Rarely reported as an incident, because the failure is the absence of governance rather than its malfunction.

name: Unauthorized or unqualified approver
plainTerms: The approval was signed by whoever was available that week, not by anyone with the authority or the background to judge it.

name: Stale approval
plainTerms: The system was approved two years ago. The vendor has swapped the underlying model twice since then. The record still says 'approved,' and technically it is.
description: A use case continues to operate under an approval that has been invalidated by a subsequent change — to the model, the vendor, the data, or the applicable regulation — because no re-review was triggered.
sectors: Cross-sector; consequences highest in banking and biopharma
indicators: Approval dates materially older than the last model or vendor change | Approval records with no expiry | Regulatory change logs with no linked re-review activity | Vendor release notes with no corresponding governance event
rootCauses: Approvals modelled as one-time events rather than time-boxed states | No structural linkage between change management and the approval record | No owner monitoring regulatory change against the existing portfolio
mitigations: Time-box every approval with a defined expiry | Trigger re-review on model, vendor, data, or regulatory change | Link change records to approval records structurally rather than by convention | Operate a regulatory-change-to-portfolio impact process
reference: Typically surfaced during examination or inspection rather than as a publicly reported incident.

name: Use outside approved scope
plainTerms: A tool approved to draft internal summaries is now generating content that goes to customers. No new approval was sought, because to everyone involved it felt like the same tool doing the same thing.
description: A system approved for one narrow purpose is progressively used for others. Each extension appears minor in isolation; the cumulative result is a system operating well outside its assessed and approved risk profile.
sectors: Manufacturing, insurance, banking, professional services
indicators: Usage patterns diverging from the documented intended-use statement | New user groups onboarded with no corresponding governance event | Output types appearing that were absent from the original assessment | Vendor capability expansion adopted without re-intake
rootCauses: No documented use-case boundary statement exists to be breached | Success in the approved use invites informal extension | Nothing monitors actual usage against approved scope
mitigations: Require an explicit use-case boundary statement at the point of approval | Monitor usage against declared boundaries | Define re-intake triggers for scope extension | Treat vendor capability changes as a governance event
reference: Commonly identified during internal audit rather than through public incident reporting.

name: Conditional-approval conditions never verified
plainTerms: Approval was granted on condition the team added human review and logging before launch. They launched. Nobody ever checked whether they added either.
description: Approval is granted subject to conditions — add human review, implement logging, complete testing before launch. The conditions are recorded in the approval and then never checked. The system operates as though fully approved while the basis of that approval was never satisfied.
sectors: Cross-sector; most consequential in banking, insurance and biopharma
indicators: Approvals containing conditions with no corresponding verification record | No field distinguishing conditional approval from unconditional | Conditions expressed as prose in a comment rather than as tracked items | No owner or due date attached to any condition | Systems in production whose approval conditions remain open
rootCauses: Conditions captured as narrative text rather than as tracked obligations | No mechanism links a condition to a verification event | Conditional approval treated as approval, because operationally it releases the same permissions | The reviewer who set the condition has no visibility after the decision
mitigations: Record each condition as a tracked item with an owner and a due date | Distinguish conditional from unconditional approval in the record and in reporting | Require positive verification evidence before a condition is closed | Escalate overdue conditions on the same basis as overdue findings | Report open conditions on deployed systems as a standing metric
reference: Structurally identical to the findings-and-remediation failures in TA11, but occurring at the approval gate rather than after review. Organizations frequently fix one and not the other.

name: No defined responsibility model for approval
plainTerms: Four people have to sign off. None of them can say which parts they are each responsible for, so each waits to see what the others do first.

name: Approval without substantive review
plainTerms: The committee approves everything. Nobody can recall the last time a request was sent back with a material objection.

name: Emergency approval with no subsequent review
plainTerms: Something urgent got approved in a hallway conversation to hit a deadline. The proper review was going to happen right after launch. That was a year ago.

name: No service level on review decisions
plainTerms: Teams submit a request and hear nothing for six weeks. There's no published turnaround time, so nothing is ever technically late — and people stop waiting and start improvising.
description: No committed turnaround exists for governance decisions. Because nothing is late by definition, delay is never escalated, never measured, and never treated as a defect. The predictable consequence is that teams route around governance rather than wait for it.
sectors: Cross-sector
indicators: No published turnaround commitment for any review stage | Submitters contacting reviewers directly to ask about status | Items with no status change for extended periods and no escalation triggered | Pent-up demand visible as a surge whenever a fast path is announced | Rising discovery of deployed systems that never entered review
rootCauses: Governance designed around thoroughness with no throughput commitment | No owner of end-to-end cycle time | Escalation paths defined for risk but not for delay | Capacity constraints treated as immovable rather than as a governable parameter
mitigations: Publish service levels per review tier and report performance against them | Trigger automatic escalation when an item exceeds its service level | Operate a regular triage cadence rather than ad-hoc scheduling | Make cycle time a reported governance metric alongside risk metrics | Treat sustained service-level breach as a finding, not as background noise
reference: Presents as shadow adoption and submitter attrition rather than as a reportable incident. The causal link between review latency and unsanctioned use is the most consistent pattern in this catalog.

name: No precedent reuse
plainTerms: The same question — can we use this kind of model with this kind of data — has now been answered eight times by eight different reviewers. There's no record of the previous answers, so the ninth team starts from scratch.
description: Each review is conducted from first principles because prior decisions are not captured in reusable form. Reviewer effort is spent re-deriving conclusions that already exist, decisions drift as different reviewers reach different answers to the same question, and the organization cannot demonstrate consistency of treatment.
sectors: Cross-sector; compounding cost rises with portfolio size
indicators: Reviewers unable to cite a prior decision on a materially identical question | Similar use cases receiving different conditions or outcomes | No searchable repository of past decisions, guidance, or accepted patterns | Review duration not decreasing as volume increases
rootCauses: Decisions recorded as approvals rather than as reasoning | No repository for guidance, patterns, or reference architectures | Review treated as a per-item task rather than as an accumulating knowledge base | Reviewer turnover with no capture of accumulated judgement
mitigations: Maintain a searchable repository of decisions, guidance, and accepted patterns | Record the reasoning, not only the outcome | Define pre-approved patterns that qualifying use cases can adopt without full review | Publish playbooks for recurring use-case archetypes | Measure the proportion of reviews resolved by precedent as a programme health metric
reference: Presents as persistent reviewer load and inconsistent treatment of comparable cases.

name: Review sequencing mismatch
plainTerms: Review step three requires test results that only get produced at step five. Every request reaches step three, gets sent back, and goes around again. Everyone involved knows. Nobody has changed the order.
description: Governance gates are ordered so that an earlier stage requires artifacts produced by a later one. Items cycle repeatedly between stages, consuming reviewer capacity and elapsed time without adding assurance. The failure is structural: no amount of additional effort or resourcing resolves it, because the loop is built into the sequence.
sectors: Cross-sector; most visible in organizations with formal multi-stage review
indicators: Items repeatedly transitioning backward between the same two stages | Reviewers routinely rejecting for missing artifacts rather than for substance | Average number of stage transitions materially exceeding the number of stages | Teams pre-emptively producing artifacts out of sequence to avoid the loop | Stage-level metrics that look healthy while end-to-end cycle time does not
rootCauses: Stages designed independently by the functions that own them | No end-to-end process owner with authority to reorder gates | Artifact dependencies never mapped against stage sequence | Loop normalized over time and re-described as 'how the process works'
mitigations: Map artifact dependencies against stage order and reorder where they conflict | Introduce an explicit stage for producing prerequisite artifacts before the gate requiring them | Assign end-to-end process ownership with authority to change sequencing | Instrument backward transitions as a first-class metric | Review process design when backward transition rates exceed a defined threshold
reference: Widely experienced, rarely documented — the loop is usually described as a resourcing problem rather than a design defect.

name: Missing human-in-the-loop trigger
plainTerms: The policy says a person reviews every high-value decision. In the actual system, there is no screen where a person could do that, and no record that anyone ever has.
description: A decision pathway that requires human review under policy or law has no mechanism that enforces the review. The system decides and acts autonomously in cases where a human was supposed to intervene.
sectors: Banking (credit, fraud), insurance (claims), employment screening, healthcare
indicators: Decision logs containing no human-review event | Automated approval rates at or near 100% | No reviewer identity captured on high-impact decisions | Review queue depth of zero on a pathway that should be generating reviews
rootCauses: Human oversight specified in policy prose but never implemented as a system control | Review thresholds defined qualitatively and therefore unenforceable | Volume pressure leads to the checkpoint being disabled without a governance decision
mitigations: Define review thresholds numerically and enforce them in the system | Make the checkpoint blocking rather than advisory | Run sampling audits of automated decisions to confirm the pathway operates | Capture and retain reviewer identity as evidence
reference: A recurring contributing factor across publicly reported automated-decision harms in the AI Incident Database.

name: Human review present but not substantive
plainTerms: There is a review step. The reviewer processes four hundred items an hour. It is a button, not a judgement.

name: Orphaned ownership
plainTerms: The person who built and owned the system left in March. The system is still running, still making decisions, and has no owner.
description: A deployed system has no current owner. The person who built or sponsored it has left, changed role, or moved team, and ownership was never reassigned. The system continues to operate, make decisions, and consume data with nobody accountable for it.
sectors: Cross-sector; prevalence rises with organizational change frequency
indicators: Register entries whose named owner no longer appears in the directory | Owner fields populated with a team name rather than a person | Systems with no governance activity for an extended period | Review requests returning undeliverable | No reassignment step in the leaver or internal-transfer process
rootCauses: Ownership captured at intake and never revisited | Offboarding processes cover access and equipment but not governance ownership | Reassignment has no trigger, so it depends on someone noticing | Ownership recorded as an individual with no defined successor or accountable role
mitigations: Trigger ownership reassignment from the leaver and internal-transfer processes | Record an accountable role alongside the named individual | Run periodic ownership attestation across the register | Report unowned systems as a standing exception | Block approval renewal on a system with no current owner
reference: Frequently discovered during an audit or an incident, when someone needs to reach the owner and finds there is not one.

name: No escalation path
plainTerms: Someone on the front line notices the AI is producing something wrong. There is no route for that concern to go anywhere, so they work around it and tell a colleague.

name: Diffused accountability across functions
plainTerms: A decision needs risk, legal, data, and the business to agree. Getting them in the same room takes three weeks. The decision itself takes ten minutes.
description: Responsibility is spread across business, data, technology, legal, and risk functions with no single owner. Reviews stall in handoffs, decisions require assembling people who do not report to one another, and when something fails nobody is accountable because everybody was involved.
sectors: Cross-sector; most pronounced in large matrixed organizations
indicators: Long elapsed time against short active working time on governance reviews | Use cases stalling between functions rather than within them | No named owner recorded on a material proportion of the register | Escalations resolved by seniority rather than by defined authority
rootCauses: Governance designed as a committee rather than as a process | No responsibility model, or one that exists on paper only | Each function optimizes its own step while nobody owns end-to-end cycle time
mitigations: Publish a responsibility model with named accountable roles at each stage | Operate a single orchestration workspace so handoffs are visible | Set per-stage service levels with escalation on breach | Measure and report end-to-end cycle time rather than per-step throughput
reference: Manifests as slow delivery and unattributable failure rather than as a discrete incident.

name: No override or appeal route for affected individuals
plainTerms: A customer was declined by an automated decision. There is no way for them to ask a human to look at it again, and no one inside the company who could act if they did.

name: Governance owner without capacity
plainTerms: One person owns AI governance. It is not their only job, or their second. They are in meetings all day, and the governance work happens on weekends — or it doesn't.

name: Process communication diverges from routing logic
plainTerms: The screen tells the submitter their request is going to expert review. The rules actually send it somewhere else entirely. Nobody notices until someone goes looking for a review that never happened.

name: Undocumented data lineage
plainTerms: Ask where the training data came from and the answer is the name of a person who might remember.

name: Data-use rights and consent unverified
plainTerms: Customer data collected for billing is now training a model. Nobody checked whether customers agreed to that when they handed it over.
description: Data is used to train, tune, or prompt an AI system without anyone verifying that the organization holds the rights to use it that way. Collection for one purpose does not establish permission for another, and the check is frequently never made.
sectors: Cross-sector; acute wherever personal, customer, or licensed third-party data is involved
indicators: No recorded rights determination against any training or retrieval dataset | Privacy notices that do not contemplate AI use of the data they describe | Third-party data used in AI contexts with no licence review | Datasets whose collection basis nobody can state | Assessment forms with no data-rights question
rootCauses: Rights assessed at the point of collection and never re-assessed for new purposes | Data governance and AI governance operate as separate processes with no handoff | Assumption that internally held data is internally usable for any purpose | Licence terms for third-party data not reviewed for AI use specifically
mitigations: Require a recorded data-rights determination before any AI use of a dataset | Review privacy notices and consent bases against actual AI use | Check third-party data licences for AI, training, and derivative-work terms | Maintain a data-rights register linked to use cases | Make the rights question a blocking field on intake
reference: Among the most difficult failure modes to remediate after the fact, because retraining or rebuilding may be the only available correction.

name: Sensitive data in ungoverned tools
plainTerms: Confidential documents are being pasted into tools the company doesn't control, to get a quick summary before a meeting.

name: No data-quality gate before use
plainTerms: The model started producing strange results. It turns out the input data has been broken for five weeks. Nothing was checking.

name: Residency and cross-border rules unenforced
plainTerms: Data that is supposed to stay in one country is being processed by a service running somewhere else. Nobody set out to do that; it's just where the vendor's capacity was.

name: Retention and deletion not applied to AI artifacts
plainTerms: The company deletes customer records after seven years. The prompts and AI outputs containing those same records are kept indefinitely, because nobody classified them as records.

name: Conflicting sources of truth
plainTerms: Two dashboards show different numbers for the same thing, because they pull from two systems that disagree. Both are being used to make decisions, and nobody knows which one is right.

name: No independent validation before first use
plainTerms: The team that built the model is the team that checked whether it works.

name: Validation not proportionate to materiality
plainTerms: A model that sets pricing across the whole business received the same one-page review as a tool that reformats slides.

name: System documentation incomplete
plainTerms: The documentation is a screenshot and a sentence. Nobody outside the original team could work out what the system actually does.

name: No intended-use statement
plainTerms: There is no written statement of what the system is for, so when someone asks whether a new use is in scope, there is nothing to compare it against.

name: Assumptions and limitations undocumented
plainTerms: The model assumes customers behave the way they did three years ago. That assumption is real, load-bearing, and written down nowhere.

name: No fairness testing evidence retained
plainTerms: Fairness testing was done once, by the team that built it, in a notebook on somebody's laptop. Then the auditor asked for evidence.
description: Fairness testing was either not performed or was performed without retaining evidence in a form that satisfies an external auditor. Under several regimes the absence of evidence is itself the violation, independent of whether the system is in fact biased.
sectors: Employment screening, lending, insurance underwriting, tenant screening
indicators: No independent audit within the last twelve months on in-scope systems | Testing performed by the building team with no independence | Results held in analyst notebooks rather than in a retained record | No published summary where publication is required
rootCauses: Fairness testing treated as a build-phase activity rather than a recurring obligation | No clear determination of which systems fall in scope of which jurisdiction | Independence requirements misread as satisfied by internal second-line review
mitigations: Commission annual independent audits for in-scope automated employment decision tools | Retain evidence in an audit-ready system of record rather than in analysis artifacts | Maintain an in-scope determination register per jurisdiction | Publish required summaries on schedule
reference: Compliance studies since 2023 have repeatedly found low rates of published audit summaries among employers apparently in scope of NYC Local Law 144.

name: Generative and agentic systems governed under legacy assumptions
plainTerms: A generative assistant is being validated using the checklist written for statistical credit models. The checklist asks for things that don't apply and misses everything that does.
description: Generative and agentic systems are either forced into a validation framework designed for deterministic statistical models, or fall into a governance gap because the applicable guidance explicitly excludes them. Both produce controls that do not fit the risk.
sectors: Banking most acutely; applicable wherever legacy model risk frameworks exist
indicators: Generative use cases validated using deterministic backtesting methods | No hallucination or groundedness monitoring in place | Agent autonomy levels and tool-access scopes undocumented | Governance guidance predating generative adoption, unrevised
rootCauses: Supervisory guidance expressly places generative and agentic AI out of scope, leaving institutions to self-determine controls with no template | Existing frameworks are the only available machinery, so they are reused by default | Agentic capability changes faster than governance revision cycles
mitigations: Establish a dedicated generative and agentic standard rather than extending the model standard | Implement hallucination, groundedness, and drift monitoring appropriate to non-deterministic output | Maintain an agent registry capturing capability, autonomy level, and tool access | Define validation methods suited to probabilistic systems
reference: A structural gap rather than a discrete incident, created by the 17 Apr 2026 supersession of SR 11-7 and its explicit carve-out.

name: No production-readiness gate
plainTerms: The idea was reviewed and approved at the concept stage, when it was a slide. It was then built, changed substantially along the way, and went live. Nothing looked at it again before launch.
description: Governance reviews the use case at intake but has no second checkpoint before deployment. Because most material design decisions are made after intake, the system that goes live can differ substantially from the one that was assessed — and nothing in the process is positioned to notice.
sectors: Cross-sector
indicators: Approval dates consistently preceding build start by a wide margin | No governance event recorded between approval and go-live | Deployed system characteristics differing from the intake record | Production incidents on systems whose governance record shows no issues | No defined criteria for what 'ready to deploy' requires
rootCauses: Governance programme built intake-first, with later lifecycle stages never implemented | Assumption that intake approval covers the whole lifecycle | Deployment owned by delivery teams with no governance touchpoint | No agreed production-readiness criteria to gate against
mitigations: Establish an explicit production-readiness review distinct from intake approval | Define readiness criteria covering monitoring, human oversight, rollback, and documentation | Require confirmation that the deployed system matches the assessed system | Gate deployment access or release approval on the readiness review | Treat material design change during build as a re-assessment trigger
reference: Commonly identified when a production incident traces back to a system whose governance record appears complete because it was assessed at concept stage.

name: No change control over model, prompt or vendor changes
plainTerms: Someone changed the prompt driving a customer-facing assistant. It was a two-line edit. There's no record of who, when, or why, and no way to get back to the old one.

name: Silent vendor model update
plainTerms: The vendor upgraded their model over a weekend. Output quality changed noticeably on Monday. Nobody was told in advance and nothing was re-checked afterwards.
description: A vendor changes the model underneath a deployed system without advance notice. Behaviour shifts, output quality moves, and the organization discovers it from downstream effects rather than from the vendor. Nothing in the governance record marks the change.
sectors: Cross-sector; universal wherever AI capability is consumed as a service
indicators: Output quality or behaviour shifting with no corresponding internal change | Vendor release notes that postdate the behaviour change | No contractual notice requirement for model changes | No monitoring baseline against which a change would be visible | Model version absent from the governance record
rootCauses: Model updates treated by the vendor as routine service maintenance | No contractual notice requirement negotiated at procurement | No performance baseline, so change is invisible rather than merely unannounced | Model version not captured in the record, so there is nothing to compare against
mitigations: Negotiate advance notice of model changes into vendor contracts | Record the specific model version in the governance record and monitor for drift from it | Maintain a performance baseline sensitive enough to detect behavioural change | Pin model versions where the vendor supports it | Treat a detected vendor change as a re-review trigger
reference: The clearest case in the catalog of a governance failure originating outside the organization. The failure is not the vendor change; it is the absence of any mechanism that would notice one.

name: Change misclassified as non-material
plainTerms: 'We just switched models' was logged as a minor configuration change, so it skipped review entirely.

name: No rollback plan
plainTerms: The new version is behaving badly. There is no agreed, tested way to go back to the old one, so the choice is to leave it running or turn it off.

name: Environment drift between test and production
plainTerms: It worked in testing. Production has different data, different settings, and different permissions, so it doesn't.

name: Governance tooling configuration drift
plainTerms: The governance workflow in the test system and the one in the live system aren't the same. Records moved between them quietly lose fields, and items disappear from the queues people actually work from.

name: Absent or undocumented drift review
plainTerms: The model's accuracy has been sliding for eight months. Nobody looked, because looking wasn't anybody's job.
description: Model or system performance is not monitored for degradation over time, or is monitored informally without retained evidence. Performance decays silently until it surfaces as a business failure or an audit finding.
sectors: Cross-sector; regulatory consequence highest in banking and biopharma
indicators: No documented drift review within the defined review period | Monitoring dashboards with no owner and no review record | Performance thresholds undefined, so nothing can breach | Alerting configured but routed to an unmonitored channel
rootCauses: Monitoring treated as a technical function detached from governance | No thresholds defined at approval, so there is no baseline to drift from | No named owner and no service level for review
mitigations: Define quantitative performance thresholds at the point of approval | Schedule drift reviews producing retained, dated evidence | Assign a named monitoring owner with a defined service level | Route alerting to a monitored, accountable channel
reference: Among the most frequently cited technical contributors across AI Incident Database entries involving deployed production systems.

name: No performance thresholds defined
plainTerms: Everyone agrees performance should be monitored. Nobody has said what 'bad' looks like, so nothing ever triggers and the monitoring is decorative.

name: No AI-incident definition or reporting channel
plainTerms: Something went wrong with an AI system. Nobody was sure whether it counted as an incident, or who to tell, so it was handled as a bug.
description: The organization has no working definition of what constitutes an AI incident and no channel for reporting one. Events that would trigger regulatory reporting obligations elsewhere are handled as ordinary defects, and the reporting clock runs without anyone knowing it has started.
sectors: Cross-sector; regulatory consequence highest for EU-facing high-risk deployments
indicators: No written definition of an AI incident | AI failures resolved through the standard defect process with no governance visibility | No named recipient for an AI incident report | Staff unable to say who they would tell | No log of AI incidents, which is usually read as an absence of incidents
rootCauses: Incident processes designed for security and availability, not for AI behaviour | No agreed threshold distinguishing a defect from an incident | Reporting obligations not mapped to internal triggers | Fear that logging incidents creates exposure, so they are logged as defects
mitigations: Publish a written definition of an AI incident with worked examples | Route AI incidents through a channel with governance visibility, not only engineering | Map external reporting obligations and deadlines to internal detection triggers | Capture near-misses alongside incidents | Rehearse the reporting path before it is needed
reference: The reporting deadlines under Art. 73 are measured in days. An organization without a detection and escalation path will generally exhaust them before the obligation is recognized.

name: No feedback loop from incidents into governance
plainTerms: The same problem has happened three times. Each time it was fixed. Nothing changed in how things get approved, so it will happen a fourth time.

name: No monitoring owner or service level
plainTerms: There's a monitoring dashboard. It's genuinely good. No one has opened it since the week it was built.

name: Near-misses uncaptured
plainTerms: The system nearly caused a serious error and somebody caught it by luck. It was fixed quietly and never written down, so the luck isn't reproducible.

name: No stage-aging or cycle-time metric
plainTerms: Leadership asks how long approvals are taking. The system can show which stage each item is in, but not how long it's been sitting there — so the real answer is a guess, and it's usually optimistic.

name: Evidence gap at audit
plainTerms: Every control worked exactly as designed. The auditor asked for proof. The proof was in someone's email, someone else's chat, and a folder nobody could find.
description: A control operated correctly but was not documented in a producible form, so compliance cannot be demonstrated at examination or inspection. The organization did the right thing and still receives the finding.
sectors: Banking, biopharma, insurance — anywhere external examination occurs
indicators: Evidence assembled reactively in the weeks preceding an examination | Controls described in policy with no corresponding artifact | Evidence scattered across email, chat, and personal drives | Prior findings citing documentation rather than control design
rootCauses: Evidence capture is manual and therefore skipped under operational load | No single system of record, so evidence has no natural home | Controls designed for operation rather than for demonstrability
mitigations: Capture evidence in a system of record at the moment the control operates | Link every control explicitly to its evidence artifact | Collect continuously rather than reactively | Design controls to be demonstrable, not merely effective
reference: A common category of finding in model and AI governance examinations, where the deficiency is evidentiary rather than operational.

name: No single system of record
plainTerms: AI governance records live in a spreadsheet, a ticketing system, three inboxes and a shared drive. There is no single place that is authoritative, so every question has several answers.

name: No regulatory mapping maintained
plainTerms: The company has controls. Nobody has mapped which control satisfies which regulatory requirement, so every audit starts from zero and takes six weeks.

name: Reactive evidence assembly
plainTerms: Six weeks before the examination, four people stop their day jobs to reconstruct evidence for the previous two years.

name: No periodic re-attestation
plainTerms: Systems were approved once. There is no point at which anyone is asked to confirm they're still appropriate, still used as described, or still needed.

name: No portfolio-level visibility
plainTerms: The board asks how many AI systems the company runs. The honest answer is that nobody knows.
description: Governance operates case by case with no aggregated view. Leadership cannot state how many AI systems exist, what their combined risk profile is, or where concentrations sit — so risk is managed locally and never in aggregate.
sectors: Cross-sector; consequence rises with portfolio size
indicators: No current count of AI systems in production | Risk reported per use case and never at portfolio level | No catalog of deployed solutions | Board reporting assembled manually each cycle
rootCauses: Governance built for individual approvals rather than portfolio management | Records held across disconnected systems | No aggregate risk methodology defined
mitigations: Maintain a solutions catalog as the authoritative portfolio view | Provide standing executive reporting rather than assembled reporting | Define and apply a portfolio-level risk aggregation method | Track concentration by vendor, model family, and business function
reference: Surfaces as an inability to answer supervisory or board questions rather than as an operational incident.

name: Historical attribution lost through organizational change
plainTerms: A reorganization moved people between teams. Historical records now show the new structure, so reports about last year's reviews no longer match what actually happened — and the reviewers who did the work have vanished from their own reviews.
description: Governance records reflect the current organizational structure rather than the structure in place when the work was performed. Reorganizations, departures, and role changes silently rewrite the historical record, so past reviews can no longer be attributed to the people and functions that actually conducted them.
sectors: Cross-sector; severity rises with organizational change frequency and portfolio age
indicators: Historical reports changing values after a reorganization with no underlying record activity | Completed reviews showing reviewers who did not perform them | Departed reviewers disappearing from records they authored | Inability to reproduce a report generated before an organizational change | Reviewer fields that cannot be retired without altering historical records
rootCauses: People and organizational units modelled as live references rather than as values captured at the time | No snapshot taken when an assessment is completed | Removing a person from selection also removes them from history | Record design optimized for current-state operation, not for historical integrity
mitigations: Snapshot completed assessments so historical values are fixed at completion | Distinguish archiving from deletion — retire people from future selection while preserving past attribution | Maintain an active/inactive status distinct from presence in the record | Retain organizational attribution as recorded at the time of the work | Test reproducibility of historical reports as part of any organizational change
reference: Rarely recognized until an examination requires reproducing a report from before a reorganization.

name: Governance data model too rigid to record reality
plainTerms: The system allows two findings per review. Real reviews routinely produce five. The other three are recorded in a spreadsheet, or not at all — so the official record understates what was actually found.

name: Manual bulk remediation of governance records
plainTerms: Correcting several hundred governance records has to be done by hand, one at a time, because nothing can safely update them in bulk. Everyone involved knows some of them will end up wrong.

name: Findings tracked outside the system of record
plainTerms: The review produced eleven action items. They live in a spreadsheet on a shared drive. Whether any of them have been done is anyone's guess.
description: Review findings are recorded outside the governance system — typically in spreadsheets, documents, or email threads — so they are disconnected from the use case they concern, invisible in reporting, and dependent on an individual to chase. The review process functions; the remediation process does not exist as a process at all.
sectors: Cross-sector; the most common gap between programmes that appear mature and programmes that are
indicators: Action items maintained in spreadsheets or documents rather than in the governance record | No way to report open findings without manual compilation | Status updates obtained by individually contacting owners | Findings with no traceable link to the use case that generated them | Items whose current status nobody can state without asking someone
rootCauses: Governance tooling implemented for intake and review, with remediation never scoped | Findings treated as an output of review rather than as a tracked object | No owner of the remediation process distinct from the review process | Spreadsheet adopted as a stopgap and never replaced
mitigations: Record findings as first-class objects within the governance system of record | Link every finding to its originating review and use case | Generate portfolio-level open-findings reporting as standing output | Automate status requests rather than relying on individual follow-up | Treat the remediation loop as in scope when implementing governance tooling
reference: Presents at audit as an inability to demonstrate that identified issues were resolved.

name: Findings without owner or due date
plainTerms: The finding says 'improve monitoring.' It doesn't say who, or by when, so it belongs to everyone and therefore to no one.
description: A finding is recorded without a named owner or a date by which it must be resolved. It belongs to everyone and therefore to nobody, cannot be chased, cannot age, and cannot appear on any credible overdue report.
sectors: Cross-sector
indicators: Findings with empty owner or due-date fields | Owners recorded as a team or function rather than a person | No overdue report, because nothing can be overdue | Findings resolved only when someone remembers them | Age of open findings unknown or uncalculated
rootCauses: Owner and due date optional rather than required at creation | Reviewers reluctant to assign work to people outside their reporting line | No agreed convention for setting due dates by severity | Findings created in a document that has no concept of ownership
mitigations: Make owner and due date mandatory at finding creation | Record a named individual, with the accountable role alongside | Set default due dates by severity so the date requires a decision to extend, not to set | Report unowned and undated findings as an exception class | Reassign automatically when an owner leaves or changes role
reference: The single cheapest failure mode in this stage to fix, and the one that unlocks escalation, ageing, and reporting.

name: No escalation on ageing findings
plainTerms: An action item has been open for seven months. Nothing happens when it ages. Nobody is notified, and it appears on no report.

name: Findings closed without evidence
plainTerms: The owner marked the item complete. There's no attachment, no link, and no description of what they actually did — just a status that changed.
description: A finding is marked complete with no artifact, link, or description of what was done. The record shows resolution; nothing demonstrates it. At audit the closure is indistinguishable from an unresolved finding that someone clicked closed.
sectors: Banking, biopharma, insurance — anywhere closure is examined externally
indicators: Closed findings with no attachment or linked artifact | Closure comments consisting of a single word | Closure rates rising sharply before reporting cycles | No field requiring evidence at closure | Closures performed by the assignee with no second party involved
rootCauses: Evidence optional rather than required at closure | Closure treated as a status change rather than as an assertion requiring proof | No independent verification step, so nothing tests the assertion | Pressure to reduce open-finding counts before a reporting date
mitigations: Require an evidence artifact or link before a finding can move to closed | Separate the assignee from the reviewer who confirms closure | Capture who confirmed closure and when, as part of the record | Sample closed findings for verification on a defined basis | Report closure-without-evidence as a control failure in its own right
reference: Closure without evidence is a common finding in regulated examinations precisely because it is invisible in internal metrics — the dashboard shows the item closed.

name: No blocked or on-hold status
plainTerms: The item is stuck waiting on somebody else, but the only available statuses are open and closed. So it looks like the owner is sitting on it, and the metrics blame the wrong person.

name: Findings not linked to the use case record
plainTerms: The finding exists. The use case it came from exists. Nothing connects them, so anyone reviewing that use case later sees a clean record.

name: No aggregate view of open findings
plainTerms: Nobody can answer how many open findings exist across the AI portfolio, how old they are, or which are overdue — so remediation is never discussed at the level where it could be resourced.

name: No challenge or rework path on remediation
plainTerms: The reviewer thinks the work isn't good enough, but the only buttons are approve and close. So they either accept something substandard or email the person and hope — and either way the record shows a clean approval.
description: The remediation workflow allows a reviewer to accept work but not to return it with a reason. Inadequate remediation is either accepted or handled informally outside the system, and in both cases the record shows an unqualified closure that nothing distinguishes from good work.
sectors: Cross-sector
indicators: No rejected or returned state in the workflow | Rework negotiated over email or chat rather than in the record | No record of any finding ever being sent back | Reviewers approving work they describe informally as incomplete | No count of rework cycles per finding
rootCauses: Workflow modelled as a linear path to closed, with no return edge | Reluctance to formally reject a colleague's work, in the absence of a neutral mechanism | Rejection assumed to be rare and therefore not designed for | Metrics reward closure rate, which a return path reduces
mitigations: Provide an explicit challenge state that returns the item to the assignee with a recorded reason | Capture rework cycles as a quality signal rather than as a failure | Distinguish first-pass acceptance from accepted-after-rework in reporting | Make the reason for return a required field so the record explains itself
reference: Effective challenge is explicit supervisory language in US model risk guidance. A workflow with no return path cannot evidence it.

name: Remediation closed by its own owner
plainTerms: The person who was asked to fix the problem is also the person who decides it was fixed. Nobody else looks. The record shows a completed action item and an approval that is really the same signature twice.
description: The assignee of a finding is also the party who closes it, with no independent confirmation. Self-certified closure is structurally the same weakness as self-validation at AGF-F060, occurring at the remediation stage instead of the validation stage.
sectors: Banking, biopharma, insurance — anywhere independence is an explicit expectation
indicators: Closure recorded by the same identity as the assignment | No reviewer field distinct from the owner field | No record of who confirmed completion | Closure timestamps identical to completion timestamps | Independence assumed from organizational distance rather than recorded
rootCauses: Workflow provides a single actor role rather than separate assignee and reviewer | Reviewer capacity treated as overhead and removed under load | Assumption that the owner is best placed to judge completion, which is true of the work and not of the assurance | No policy stating who may close what
mitigations: Separate assignee and reviewer as distinct required roles in the workflow | Prevent the assignee from performing the closing action on their own item | Record reviewer identity and timestamp as part of the closure | Scale independence to severity — critical findings reviewed outside the owning function | Sample self-closed historical items where the separation was introduced late
reference: Independence of review is one of the oldest expectations in regulated assurance. Its absence in AI remediation workflows is usually a tooling limitation rather than a policy decision.
